solution:
Write the complex as \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_2\). The square brackets mark the coordination sphere, and only what lies outside them can ionise in water.

The six \(\text{NH}_3\) molecules are neutral ligands bonded to the metal through coordinate bonds, so they stay attached to cobalt and never appear as separate particles. Both chlorides lie outside the brackets as counter-ions, held by ionic attraction alone, so water separates them completely. Since \(\text{NH}_3\) carries no charge, the charge on the complex ion equals the oxidation state of the metal: two chlorides must be balanced, so cobalt is \(\text{Co}^{2+}\) and the cation is \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}\).

Dissolution therefore gives \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_2 \longrightarrow [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 2\,\text{Cl}^-\) — one complex cation together with two chloride anions, a total of \(3\) ions.

Two measurements confirm the count. The molar conductivity is that of a \(1:2\) electrolyte, and adding \(\text{AgNO}_3\) precipitates only \(2\) mol of \(\text{AgCl}\) per mole of complex. Counting \(6\) would require every ligand and counter-ion to break away, which coordinated ammonia does not do; counting \(2\) records the free chlorides but forgets the complex cation itself.

In all four species iron is in the \(+3\) oxidation state with a coordination number of \(6\), so neither the metal, its charge, nor the number of donor atoms can be what separates them. The difference lies in the **denticity** of the ligand.

\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(\text{NH}_3\) and \(\text{Cl}^-\) are all monodentate: each binds through a single donor atom and occupies one site, so six independent ligands are needed and any one of them can be displaced on its own. The oxalate ion \(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\) is bidentate — it donates through two oxygen atoms at once — so three oxalate ions fill all six sites, each closing a five-membered ring with the metal. That makes \([\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}\) a chelate, and the most stable of the four.

The reason is the **chelate effect**, which is largely entropic. For \([\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+} + 3\,\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \longrightarrow [\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-} + 6\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\), four particles on the left become seven on the right, so \(\Delta S\) is strongly positive and \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) becomes more negative — a larger stability constant. The ring also resists breaking: both donor atoms of a chelating ligand must detach for it to leave, and once the first bond breaks the ligand is still tethered by the second, so it usually re-attaches before it can escape.

None of the monodentate alternatives can form such a ring. \(\text{Cl}^-\) is a large, weakly basic donor that binds iron(III) only feebly; \(\text{NH}_3\) is a softer nitrogen base poorly matched to the small, hard \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) centre and is displaced by hydrolysis in aqueous solution; and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is merely the aqua ligand that oxalate replaces.
